title: The Judenrat Under Nazi Rule: Białystok’s Council Between Coercion and Resistance
summary: The council’s records expose the impossible pressures of managing labor demands, deportation threats, and survival under Nazi authority.

editorialContent:
![Białystok and the ghetto under German occupation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b2/Bialystok_Ghetto_15-20_August_1943_%28liquidation%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=api&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)

## A council formed by command

The Nazi-imposed Jewish Council in Białystok was not a government chosen freely by its residents. It was an institution created under occupation to transmit German orders—and to manage the community forced to live with them. The memorial book’s account begins on June 29, 1941, when the German commandant summoned Rabbi Gedaliah Rozenman and community director and engineer Efraim Barash, ordering them to form a council. Soon, it says, a body of 24 people, including two women, had been appointed. Its account names, among others, Gedaliah Rozenman, [Efraim Barash](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_94cb079e0e3fc9a91fabbf23), [Jacob Lifshits](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_2600734539757f4a6105bd46), and [Cwi Wider](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_9208e11288012f91fd242948). [The council’s formation](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_2de3739b3a494a3df912c4dc) drew on people already known in communal, religious, social, and cultural life.

The memorial book distinguishes between the council’s formal leadership and its practical center of power. Rozenman was named chairman, but Barash, his deputy, became the council’s actual leader; Rozenman later withdrew from much of the daily work because of age and poor health. Yad Vashem’s biographical account supports this outline: it says the Germans first named Rabbi Rosenmann chairman and that Barash ran the council as his deputy before formally taking over about a month later. Barash, a Zionist and former executive director of the Jewish community, had moved to Białystok in 1934. ([Yad Vashem, “Barasz, Efraim”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%205972.pdf))

The sources differ in details of the council’s beginnings: the memorial book gives a 24-member council, while a later recovered-protocol account in the book refers to a “newly elected” body in August 1941. The sequence suggests that the council’s composition or formal organization changed; it cautions against treating its first days as a single settled administrative moment.

## Orders, services, and the promise of work

The Germans used the council as an instrument of rule. The memorial book describes labor demands arriving even before the council was fully organized, along with orders to surrender valuables and goods. Its account of the council records a daily reality in which officials had to collect resources and answer German demands while residents faced forced labor, hunger, crowding, and danger. The council also ran departments and services—among them sanitation, social aid, and cultural work—and created a Jewish police force under German authority. The council’s [work and labor administration](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_9208e11288012f91fd242948) and [police](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_1366452c7e2e4f9d087b0006) were therefore part of both communal administration and the coercive machinery imposed on the ghetto.

The [Białystok Ghetto](/communities/bialystok/records/mention_fa4cc4135827db4d1d8daab0) was established in 1941. The US Holocaust Memorial Museum estimates that about 50,000 Jews from the city and surrounding region were confined there; many were forced to work, particularly in textile factories. The council’s strategy increasingly centered on making the ghetto’s workforce and industries useful to German authorities. Barash believed that productive labor might preserve lives by making the ghetto indispensable. This was not a guarantee but a desperate calculation made under German control. ([USHMM, “Bialystok”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok); [Yad Vashem, “Barasz, Efraim”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%205972.pdf))

A revealing voice survives in a protocol reproduced by Yad Vashem. A Jewish police official complains about curfew violations, yellow badges, blackouts, street trading, and people avoiding work, warning that disobedience might provoke a “catastrophe.” The passage shows how German threats could be repeated through Jewish institutions, even as officials tried to prevent punishments they could not control. ([Yad Vashem, protocol of a Judenrat session](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%204682.pdf))

## Two orders for “twelve thousand”

The memorial book records a particularly painful council decision: in 1941, before Rosh Hashanah, German authorities ordered about 12,000 Jews removed from Białystok. The book says the council held a long, difficult meeting to decide who would be included. It describes a proposed selection involving poor and non-working residents, communal dwellings, and lists—decisions made under German pressure that still placed choices about individual lives in Jewish hands. The memory of that order is captured in [the account of planning the removal](/communities/bialystok/records/event_candidate_06710533c37dd235c46b4874) and [the order to remove 12,000 Jews](/communities/bialystok/records/event_candidate_5598be44f6d57c7dd6c6d876).

That episode must not be confused with another demand for 12,000, described in the memorial book’s account of the February 1943 deportation. There, rumors spread in late January that Barash had been ordered to prepare a list of 12,000 people, ostensibly for labor; the list, according to the account, included the elderly, sick, and unemployed. The two episodes differ in date and context: one belongs to 1941, the other to the February 1943 Aktion. They are not a single event repeated with a changed date.

The USHMM records the February 1943 deportation as approximately 10,000 Jews sent to Treblinka, with hundreds killed during the operation. Yad Vashem’s Barash biography gives a range of 9,000–10,000 “nonproductive” Jews deported. These outside accounts broadly confirm the scale of the 1943 deportation, but they do not erase the distinction between it and the earlier 1941 removal order. ([USHMM, “Bialystok”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok); [Yad Vashem, “Barasz, Efraim”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%205972.pdf))

## Barash, the underground, and the limits of protection

Barash’s policy was neither simple collaboration nor uncomplicated resistance. The memorial book presents a leader focused on keeping people alive through work and negotiation, but it also preserves sharp criticism of the council’s choices. Its later account says resistance leader Mordechai Tenenbaum obtained copies of council records with Barash’s consent. Yad Vashem adds that Barash helped fund weapons production and cooperated with Tenenbaum, while also noting that their relationship broke down shortly before the uprising. The record makes clear that the council and underground were not simply two unified camps: they could cooperate in secret while disagreeing over whether armed resistance would save lives or hasten collective destruction. ([Yad Vashem, “Barasz, Efraim”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%205972.pdf); [USHMM, “Jewish Councils (Judenraete)”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/jewish-councils-judenraete))

The council’s archive itself became part of this struggle. The memorial book reports that Barash allowed Tenenbaum and other underground activists to copy council minutes and announcements. It says recovered protocols and notices later documented the ghetto’s administration and daily life. These records offer more than a portrait of leaders: they show how residents were addressed, what regulations were imposed, and how officials understood the dangers around them. The route from council office to underground archive is a thread worth following through [the recovered protocols and announcements](https://www.jewishgen.org/yizkor/Bialystok1/biay187.html).

Barash’s belief in labor as protection grew more fragile as other ghettos in the region were liquidated. The February 1943 deportation showed that work did not secure safety. In August 1943, the Germans began the final liquidation of the Białystok Ghetto; armed resistance followed, and the revolt was crushed after five days. Yad Vashem reports that Barash and other council members were deported to Majdanek, and that the exact details of his death are unknown. ([Yad Vashem, “Barasz, Efraim”](https://wwv.yadvashem.org/odot_pdf/Microsoft%20Word%20-%205972.pdf); [USHMM, “Bialystok”](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/bialystok))

## Remembering without simplifying

The memorial book’s testimony is not a verdict delivered from outside the ghetto. It preserves the arguments, actions, and painful consequences recalled by survivors. The broader historical record places Białystok within a wider Nazi system: Jewish councils were ordered to implement German policies, while also trying to sustain basic community services. As the USHMM emphasizes, their members faced impossible dilemmas, and the history of the councils remains controversial. In Białystok, the record shows both the burden of decisions made under force and the efforts—sometimes hidden—to aid resistance.

The names matter because the institution was made of people: Rozenman, Barash, Wider, Lifshits, and many others whose roles and fates cannot all be reconstructed from one account. The memorial book is a vital witness to what the community remembered, but it cannot account for everyone displaced, killed elsewhere, or absent from its pages. A fuller history depends on reading its testimony alongside protocols, archival records, and independent scholarship—and on resisting the false comfort of a simple judgment.
